Microsoft and Meta reported the same day, spent on the same thing, and got opposite verdicts. Microsoft's up 8% because Azure crossed $100 billion and cloud growth hit its fastest clip since 2022 — the AI capex showed up as a number a customer actually paid. Meta's down 10% because the same kind of spending flattened its free cash flow, and Zuckerberg's response was to start hinting at a cloud business of its own. That's not a growth story. That's a company quietly admitting it built more compute than its ad business can absorb, and now needs someone else to help cover the electric bill. Same line item on the balance sheet, completely different sentence attached to it.

Then the GDP print: 1.5% growth, weaker than expected, inflation still sitting above target. Not a crisis, just an unglamorous stagflation-shaped number, landing the same week the Fed held rates after what reporters are calling a cliffhanger with three dissents. And investors are already saying Warsh's stripped-down communication style — the one Wall Street nicknamed WarshGPT a couple weeks ago, building models just to guess what he's not saying — is backfiring. Turns out when the growth-and-inflation picture actually gets murky, people want the Fed chair to say more, not less. Silence only reads as confidence when everyone already agrees on the story underneath it.

Both threads rhyme, oddly. Nobody's grading the spend, or the policy, on vibes anymore. Show the receipts, or the market writes its own version of your sentence for you.
